grammar.title: Question words
grammar.summary: Question words like bin1 go3? who? and mat1 je5? what? come in the same position in the sentence as the answer to them does.
grammar.body:
Question words like bin1-go3? who? and mat1-je5? what? come in the same position in the sentence as the answer to them does. In English question and answer have different word orders, but in Chinese they have the same word order. In the two examples following note how the English is twisted but the Chinese is not.
Some people say mi1 je5? instead of mat1 je5?: there is no difference in meaning.
Note how aa3 is used at the end of sentences which are questions.

examples.jp: A: keoi5 sing3 mat1 je5 aa3?
A: keoi5 wan2 bin1 go3 aa3?
B: keoi5 wan2 Ho4 siu2 ze2
examples.en: She is looking for Miss Ho

grammar.title: Possession: ge3
grammar.summary: The little word ge3 shows possession, like the apostrophe s ('s) in English.
grammar.body: The little word “ge3” shows possession, like the apostrophe s (’s) in English.

grammar.title: Ge3 is used in two ways
grammar.summary: Ge3 comes before a possessed noun, or stands as a predicate, usually following the verb hai6 'to be'.
grammar.body:
Before a possessed noun (ngo5 ge3 dei6 zi2 my address; Wong4 taai3 taai2 ge3 ce1 Mrs. Wong's car).
As predicates, usually following the verb hai6 ‘to be’ (ni1 go3 hai6 nei5 ge3 this is yours).

examples.jp: ngo5 ge3 dei6 zi2 hai2 ni1 dou6
nei5 ge3 gwong2 dung1 waa2 m4 co3
keoi5 ge3 gin6 hong1 m4 hai6 gei2 hou2
examples.en: Her health is not too good

examples.jp: zi6 gei2 ge3 gaa1 ting4 zeoi3 gan2 jiu3
examples.en: One's own family is most important

examples.jp: Ngo5 dei6 ge3 se2 zi6 lau4
Ce1 hai6 Wong4 siu2 ze2 ge3
Zung1 gwok3 ce1 hai6 keoi5 ge3

grammar.title: Ge3: omitting hai6, and close relationships
grammar.summary: The verb hai6 can be understood from context and omitted; with close personal relationship terms of two or more syllables, ge3 itself is often left out.
grammar.body:
The verb hai6 can be understood from the context, so sometimes it's omitted (baa2 ze1 keoi5 ge3 this umbrella is hers).
When there is a close personal relationship with a person, ge3 is often left out, but the relationship term must have at least two syllables, as with taai3 taai2 and pang4 jau5 (keoi5 sai3 lou2 her younger brother).

examples.jp: ni1 tiu4 so2 si4 bin1 go3 ge3?

grammar.title: Ge3: possessor phrases
grammar.summary: Relationship phrases like keoi5 sai3 lou2 can themselves serve as the possessor of another noun, followed by ge3.
grammar.body: These phrases can themselves serve as the possessor of another noun (keoi5 sai3 lou2 ge3 man6 tai4 her younger brother's problems).

examples.jp: keoi5 sai3 lou2 ge3 man6 tai4 hou2 do1
examples.en: Her younger brother's problems are many

examples.jp: ngo5 lou5 gung1 ge3 nguk1 kei2 jan4 lai4 saai3
examples.en: My husband's family have all come

examples.jp: nei5 gu1 ze1 ge3 mat6 jip6 hou2 zik6 cin2
examples.en: Your aunt's property is worth a lot of money

grammar.title: Classifier in place of ge3; plural di1
grammar.summary: Before nouns the appropriate classifier is often used instead of ge3, denoting a particular individual or object; for more than one, the plural classifier di1 is used.
grammar.body:
Before nouns, the appropriate classifier is often used in place of ge3, especially in colloquial language (ngo5 go3 neoi2 my daughter).
This has a similar meaning to the corresponding phrase with ge3, but denotes a particular individual or object.
To specify more than one, the plural classifier di1 is used (ngo5 di1 zai2 neoi2 my children).

grammar.title: Thank you: m4 goi1
grammar.summary: m4 goi1 literally means 'not ought to', but it is the most common word for thank you.
grammar.body:
m4 goi1 literally means “not ought to”, but it is the most common word for thank you.
If someone holds the door open for you, passes you the soy sauce or tells you your shoelace is undone, you should politely say m4 goi1 to them.

grammar.title: Hai6 vs. hai2
grammar.summary: hai6 means 'be' (identity); hai2, with a different tone, means 'be at/in/on' (location).
grammar.body:
Notice the difference in tone between hai6 and hai2, which can also be translated as ‘be’ but in the sense of being located.
hai6 = be; hai2 = be at/in/on.

grammar.title: Classifiers
grammar.summary: In Cantonese, this, that, which? and numbers must be followed by a classifier word before the noun.
grammar.body:
In English when you specify a word with this, that, or which?, you just put it in front of the word (this man, that ship, which pen?), but in Cantonese you need to use a classifier word as well (this classifier man, that classifier ship, which classifier pen?).
Classifiers pose two different problems: 1. Which one to use with which noun. 2. When and where to use them.

grammar.title: Subtypes of classifiers: measures and containers
grammar.summary: Measures count quantities (pounds, catties, dozens); any container can serve as a measure; container words used as nouns take the classifier go3.
grammar.body:
Measures: words used in counting quantities as in “two dozen eggs” (loeng5 bong6 ngau4 juk6 two pounds of beef).
Containers: these form an open-ended category since any container can serve as a measure (saam1 bui1 caa4 three cups of tea).
These container words can also be used as nouns, in which case they take the classifier go3 (jat1 go3 wun2 a bowl).

grammar.title: Collective classifiers
grammar.summary: Collective classifiers group items: a class, a pile, a set, a pair (deoi3). Not everything that is a pair in English takes deoi3.
grammar.body:
A grouping of items (ni1 baan1 hok6 saang1 this class of students; jat1 daap6 syu1 a pile of books; go2 deoi3 haai4 that pair of shoes).
Not all things that are treated as pairs in English take deoi3: ‘a pair of trousers’ is jat1 tiu4 fu3, ‘a pair of scissors’ jat1 baa2 gaau3 zin2.
On the other hand, there are other uses of deoi3 which are understandable (ngo5 deoi3 sau2 my (two) hands).

grammar.title: Which classifier? Semantic classes
grammar.summary: Classifiers generally serve to sort nouns into semantic classes of objects: baa2 tools, gaa3 vehicles, gaan1 buildings, gin6 clothes, go3 people and abstract things, zek3 animals and one of a pair.
grammar.body:
Classifiers generally serve to sort nouns into semantic classes of objects:
baa2 — tools, instruments: baa2 dou1 knife
gaa3 — machines, vehicles: gaa3 ce1 the car
gaan1 — buildings: gaan1 nguk1 the house
gin6 — most clothes: gin6 saam1 shirt, dress
go3 — people: jat1 go3 ji1 sang1 a doctor; abstract things: ni1 go3 kyut3 ding6 this decision, jat1 go3 mung6 a dream
zek3 — most animals: zek3 gau2 a dog; one of a pair: jat1 zek3 sau2 one hand

examples.en: One hand (zek3: one of a pair)

grammar.title: Which classifier? Shape
grammar.summary: Many common classifiers categorize objects by their shape: faai3 vertical surface, fuk1 square/rectangular, zoeng1 flat surface, zi1 cylindrical, lap1 small and round, tiu4 long and narrow.
grammar.body:
A further important criterion is that many common classifiers categorize objects by their shape:
faai3 — vertical surface: jat1 faai3 geng3 a mirror
fuk1 — square/rectangular: jat1 fuk1 waa2 a picture
zoeng1 — flat surface: jat1 zoeng1 toi2 a table
zi1 — cylindrical: zi1 bat1 a pen/pencil
lap1 — small and round: jat1 lap1 tong2 a sweet
tiu4 — long and narrow: tiu4 lou6 the road

grammar.title: Which classifier? Shape overrides semantic class
grammar.summary: Animals and items of clothing distinguished by their elongated shape take tiu4 rather than zek3 or gin6.
grammar.body: The shape criterion can override the semantic class criterion, so that animals and items of clothing distinguished by their elongated shape take tiu4, rather than zek3 or gin6.

grammar.title: Using classifiers: when a classifier must be used
grammar.summary: A classifier must be used (i) following a number, (ii) with the demonstratives this and that, (iii) in a possessive construction, (iv) with a noun alone.
grammar.body:
The main cases in which a classifier must be used are:
(i) following a number: jat1 go3 ji1 sang1 one doctor
(ii) with the demonstrative ‘this’ and ‘that’: ni1 go3 sai3 lou6 this child
(iii) in a possessive construction: ngo5 go3 zai2 my son
(iv) with a noun alone: go3 hok6 saang1 a/the student

grammar.title: Using classifiers: definite and indefinite
grammar.summary: Classifier + noun before the verb is definite ('the'); after the verb it can be definite or refer to an indefinite but specific item.
grammar.body:
This usage typically refers to a particular item. When the noun it goes with comes before the verb it is definite (corresponding to “the” in English).
When the classifier and noun come after the verb it can be definite, but can also refer to an indefinite, but specific item.

examples.jp: ngo5 gam1 jat6 tai2 zo2 bun2 syu1
keoi5 dei6 hoi1 zo2 go3 wu6 hau2

grammar.title: More on classifiers: dropping the noun
grammar.summary: If it is clear what is meant, the noun can be dropped, but the classifier must still be used.
grammar.body: If it is clear what is meant, it is possible to drop off the noun, but the classifier must still be used. Note the following question and answer.

examples.jp: A: nei5 jiu3 bin1 zi1 bat1 aa3

grammar.title: How about it? hou2 m4 hou2 aa3
grammar.summary: hou2 m4 hou2 aa3? literally means 'is it good?' but is also used at the end of sentences meaning 'what do you say?', 'how about it?', 'OK?'.
grammar.body:
hou2 m4 hou2 aa3? literally means is it good? But it is also used at the ends of sentences meaning what do you say?, how about it? OK?
(And there is aa3 at the end of a question sentence again!)

examples.en: What do you say? How about it? OK?

grammar.title: Numbers
grammar.summary: The numbers one to ten are single-syllable words; 11 is 10+1, 20 is 2x10, 21 is 2x10+1, and so on.
grammar.body: The Cantonese number system is very straightforward. The numbers one to ten are all single-syllable words; 11 is 10+1, 12 is 10+2, 13 is 10+3, and so on up to 20 which is 2x10; 21 is 2x10+1, 29 is 2x10+9; 30 is 3x10, 31 is 3x10+1…

grammar.title: Numbers: loeng5 vs. ji6
grammar.summary: The number two is not ji6 but loeng5 when it is followed by a classifier; complex numbers ending in two (sap6 ji6) are not affected.
grammar.body:
The whole number system is nice and regular with one exception: the number two is not ji6 but loeng5 when it is followed by a classifier.
It is only the number two itself which plays this trick; complex numbers which end in a two are not affected, as you can see from the example of sap6 ji6 zi1 bat1 twelve pens.

examples.jp: jat1 zi1 bat1, loeng5 zi1 bat1, saam1 zi1 bat1, sei3 zi1 bat1
examples.en: One pen, two pens, three pens, four pens

notes.title: The Magic of Numbers
notes.body:
Cantonese people are very interested in numbers and many people believe that numbers can influence fate.
(Lucky) baat3 eight — sounds like faat3 get rich.
(Unlucky) sei3 four — sounds like sei2 to die.
(Lucky) ji6 baat3 two eight — sounds like ji6 faat3 easy to get rich.
(Unlucky) ng5 baat3 five eight — sounds like m4 faat3 not get rich.
A Chinese buyer recently insisted on paying $280,000 for a house in the south of England rather than the asking price of $279,500 believing that the larger sum was much luckier sounding! For many years the Hong Kong government auctioned ‘lucky’ car registration numbers for charity; an astronomical price was paid for 8888, which adorned one of the territory’s many Rolls-Royces.
